name: IKEA Effect
description: People who build/assemble a product themselves value it more highly than an equivalent pre-made product — but only if the build is completed successfully.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to customization/setup flows, onboarding that involves active user input, and personalization features.
myth_risk_note: While well-replicated in laboratory settings (10.1561/107.00000039 confirms robustness), the developmental mechanisms remain incompletely understood (10.1016/j.cognition.2017.10.012 found effort-justification theory insufficient). The effect is not a zombie fact but represents an incompletely resolved theoretical picture about why labor increases valuation.
prevalence_note: A popular, memorable named concept frequently cited in onboarding/customization design discourse, though narrower in scope than the foundational-tier entries.

findings.description: Across four studies (assembling IKEA furniture, origami, Lego sets), people who built a product themselves valued it as highly as experts' finished creations and expected others to share that inflated valuation — but this effect only occurs when labor results in successful completion; it disappears if the built object is destroyed or left unfinished, and occurs equally for novices and experienced 'do-it-yourselfers.'
findings.source_title: The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love

applications.title: A parent's own IKEA-effect experiment to get kids to eat vegetables -- and its failure
applications.description: An NPR contributor, writing for the Association for Psychological Science's 'Members in the Media' series, describes deliberately invoking the IKEA effect on her own children: she gave them cut vegetables and a plain cheese pizza base to 'decorate' before baking, reasoning that self-assembly would make them value (and eat) the vegetables more. Both children enthusiastically covered their pizzas in vegetables during assembly -- then, without hesitation, picked every visible piece off before eating once the pizzas came out of the oven. The author explicitly frames this as a failed real-world application of the IKEA effect, not a success story.
applications.ethical_note: A parent's own honestly-reported anecdote about her own children, included specifically because it disconfirms a naive one-line reading of the IKEA effect ('self-assembly increases valuation') rather than because it succeeded -- useful evidentiary humility, same spirit as this graph's dialectic-verification discipline.

applications.title: A teacher and a principal use the IKEA effect deliberately to build school culture
applications.description: Writing together, a classroom teacher (Cathleen Beachboard) and a school principal (Nick Brousse) describe using the IKEA effect deliberately as a school-culture strategy: having students co-create their own classroom community principles and behavior norms (rather than being handed a rulebook), involving teacher leaders in vetting new hires so new colleagues are seen as 'our teammate' rather than 'the administration's hire,' and using student advisory groups to shape event planning and school-climate initiatives. They frame the underlying mechanism explicitly around IKEA-effect research (including findings that even young children value self-built objects more, independent of ownership or effort alone) and contrast compliance-based systems (imposed, complied with) against ownership-based ones (co-created, protected).
applications.industry_context: K-12 education, school leadership and culture
applications.ethical_note: Deliberately invoking the IKEA effect here builds genuine shared ownership and belonging among students and staff, not a manipulation of an end user for a third party's commercial benefit.

applications.title: Kids who help cook vegetables are more likely to eat them
applications.description: In a study by Radtke et al. (2019), children who were involved in cooking activities -- such as mixing ingredients, washing vegetables, or cracking eggs -- reported liking vegetables more than children who were not involved, and children who liked vegetables more also ate more of them. The finding is discussed as a real-world application of the IKEA effect: involvement in making something increases attachment to and enjoyment of the result, even for children and vegetables.
applications.ethical_note: Using the IKEA effect to help children build a genuine, lasting preference for healthy food is a clearly user-beneficial (here, child-beneficial) application with no competing commercial interest -- there is no persuasion-for-profit dimension in a parent involving their own child in cooking.
